baselineConflict.$comment: Shown on a step whose baseline source policy a review found self-contradictory (roadmap/baselineConflict.ts): one entry per reviewed source, named by that record, so the words follow the source policy and not a goal.
baselineConflict.adminPortalNonAdminScope:
The baseline says this policy should block non-admins from admin portals. But the policy it actually defines targets All users and excludes no administrator — by role, account, or group. If IAMAI followed the policy definition literally, it would lock every administrator out of the admin portals. If it followed the documentation, it would need exclusions the policy doesn't have.

IAMAI won't write instructions for either interpretation because one locks admins out and the other is incomplete. Nothing is wrong in your tenant. This step waits for the baseline author to publish a corrected version. The rest of the plan is unaffected.

scan.title: Scan
limits: Devices that send mail without signing in (Direct Send printers, scanners) leave no record; a legacy-authentication block can stop one the plan never listed. The step asks before that block enforces.
Authentication that happens outside Entra (federation, third-party MFA, on-premises apps) is recorded as a sign-in but not as what the other system enforced.
Anything on a longer cycle than the records (the quarterly invoice run, the yearly renewal) has left no evidence yet; keep new blocks in report-only across a full cycle.
Credentials saved on equipment nobody has touched in years surface the day something blocks them; a walk through the comms room beats any report.
A partner's own tenant enforces for their people; IAMAI sees their sign-ins here, never their controls.

home.metaTitle: IAMAI — Microsoft Entra Conditional Access planner
home.metaDescription: Read a Microsoft Entra tenant, see who a Conditional Access change could affect before you make it, and get a dated rollout plan. Read-only, in your browser, source public.
home.h1: Find the gaps. Catch the hidden risks. Plan a safer rollout.
home.siteLine: IAMAI looks beyond whether a policy exists. It checks the details that can make a rollout succeed or fail: which sign-in methods people have, whether the available records show they’ve used them, and whether exclusions or external accounts need attention.
home.workHeading: From a tenant scan to a dated plan you can carry out.
home.workLead: Get a practical plan for what to address first, what to check, and how to move toward stronger protection. You stay in control of every change.

work.text: A tenant's policies, people, groups, devices, licences and the last 30 days of sign-in records.
What each baseline policy is for with what the tenant already has, so a control you built yourself counts as done.
The difference as dated steps: report-only first where a policy supports it, who could be affected by each change, and the emails to send.

home.baseline: A baseline is the identity-security standard IAMAI measures your tenant against — here, a published set of Conditional Access policies, built by Jon Hope, a Microsoft MVP.
home.baselineGoal: Its aim is layered protection for a small organisation: MFA for everyone, phishing-resistant admins, constrained sessions and devices, and emergency access kept out of every policy as a backup you check and test.

stepContract.$comment: The Step Contract (Foundation D, src/ui/surfaces/stepContract.ts). Every Plan step answers the same questions in the same order: where it is now and what happens next, why, what IAMAI found, who it touches, what to do, what to fix first, how you will know it is done, and More. These are the words the contract itself supplies; each step's own sentences stay in its steps[] entry.

stepContract.$commentRailExisting: The In-place variant's own side block (task 036; docs/design/approved/plan-step-v1.html V4 draws `Existing implementation` over the policy's name). The name is Step.satisfiedBy — the coverage result that decided the goal was satisfied — so the rail names the tenant's own policy and never the baseline's. `railExistingKeep` is the sub under one sufficient policy; `railExistingTogether` is the sub where two cover the goal between them and neither covers it alone.

opening: Help me understand and carry out this IAMAI step. Explain its purpose, who it affects, how the tenant's observed state compares with the intended result, and what remains to do. Use the facts below; distinguish observations, saved decisions, proposed changes and unknowns.

Explain the next available action first, then the settings and checks needed to complete it. Point out any conflict between the instructions and the supplied policy data. If Microsoft behavior needs clarification, use current Microsoft documentation and cite the relevant page. Do not invent tenant values, approvals, completed checks or changes. Ask only for information that affects the next action.

You may explain alternatives and their tradeoffs. Clearly identify any alternative that changes the selected baseline or saved decision, and do not present it as the current plan. Do not execute a tenant change from this briefing.

how.checksIntro: Every check IAMAI runs, generated from the rules the code runs from.
limitsList: IAMAI approximates how Microsoft evaluates a sign-in; report-only is the truth. Some conditions, like device filters and token state, it cannot reproduce.
Without Entra ID P1 there is no impact analysis; the plan is licence, then security defaults, then Conditional Access.
Sign-in history shows behaviour under today's policy; it cannot see who would register MFA when first prompted.
There is no server: no scheduled re-scans, no alerts, no state shared across devices.
A sign-in session lasts about a day; the plan file never depends on it, so save the plan to keep it.

how.limitsFeedback: Something wrong or unclear? feedback@getiamai.com — I would rather hear about it than not.
how.hostingBody: getiamai.com is a static site: files on GitHub Pages, served through Cloudflare. Your tenant's data is not part of that. The scan calls Microsoft Graph from this browser and the snapshot stays here, so nothing Cloudflare or GitHub serves has ever held it. The source is public and inspectable on GitHub. One thing IAMAI does not control: Cloudflare adds its own page-load beacon to the HTML it serves. So the host measures page loads and network timing for this site. That beacon is not in IAMAI's bundle and cannot be taken out from here, only from the Cloudflare account. It measures the page, not the scan, and carries nothing from your tenant.
how.creditBaseline: The default baseline is Jon Hope's Defense in Depth, published at ConditionalAccess.Tech. IAMAI pins a reviewed version of it and reads it unchanged.
how.creditAnalyzer: CA Policy Analyzer by Jon Hope
how.creditAnalyzerNote: A separate open-source project by the same author, credited here alongside the baseline. IAMAI is a different tool and is not affiliated with it.
how.creditsNote: Microsoft MVP is an award for community contribution. It is not a Microsoft certification of this baseline, and Microsoft does not endorse or support IAMAI.

alerting.title: Alert on Emergency Account Sign-ins
alerting.why: An alert helps your team notice emergency-account use and distinguish a planned drill from unexpected access.
whatToDo: Use your approved monitoring system to alert on sign-ins by the selected emergency accounts: for example, send SignInLogs to a Log Analytics workspace (Entra admin center → Entra ID → Monitoring & health → Diagnostic settings) or the SIEM you already use.
Create an alert rule for sign-ins where UserPrincipalName is one of {list:emergencyAccountUpns}.
Send it to a monitored destination and name who responds; test it with one controlled sign-in and confirm the alert arrives.
Review ingestion, retention and cost for the monitoring service you use.
doneWhen: A controlled sign-in by an emergency account produced an alert at the monitored destination, and the response owner confirmed receipt.

hardening.title: Harden Emergency Access
hardening.why: These improvements were deferred after the minimum emergency checks passed. Completing them makes the recovery process more resilient.
whatToDo: Verify each result and scan again: the row closes when they pass. An earlier deferral does not count as done.
doneWhen: Every deferred emergency access recommendation passes on a scan.

naming.title: Rename Policies Off the Naming Convention
naming.why: Consistent names make policy reviews easier for the next person responsible for the tenant.
whatToDo: Renaming changes no Conditional Access evaluation, but scripts or reports that find policies by name may need updating; keep the same policy IDs and settings.
doneWhen: Every policy name follows {convention}.
Verify after the change: tooling that finds these policies still identifies them.

consolidation.title: Consolidate Overlapping Policies
consolidation.why: Overlapping policies can make later changes harder to understand. Consolidate only when the remaining policy preserves the access requirements that matter.
whatToDo: Compare the complete settings of {list:overlaps}: scope, exclusions, conditions, controls, risk levels and guest types.

Retire a policy only after the remaining one is shown to preserve the required coverage, tested and approved; keep a rollback record. Never remove High-risk coverage because a Medium-only policy exists.
doneWhen: Each approved retirement preserves the required coverage and has been validated through your change process.

notAssessed.title: Review Baseline Policies IAMAI Did Not Assess
notAssessed.why: Some baseline policies use settings IAMAI cannot fully assess. A manual review keeps those options available without presenting an unverified policy as complete.
whatToDo: Review each policy IAMAI could not assess, and the settings it could not compare: {list:policies}
Resolve its tenant-specific references and confirm whether it applies. Use Report-only where the policy type supports it, then the appropriate validation.
Record whether it applies, does not apply (with a reason), or still needs investigation.
doneWhen: Each policy has a recorded outcome: implemented and validated, not applicable with a reason, or still under investigation.

drill.title: Run the Emergency Access Drill
drill.why: A regular drill checks that emergency access still works before it is needed. It can reveal expired credentials, missing roles or an alert nobody receives.
whatToDo: For each emergency account, in your approved secure recovery environment: retrieve its credentials through the authorized process, sign in, perform a non-destructive administrative check, confirm the expected logs and alert, and sign out.
Record the full result and date in the plan file. Repeat at least every 90 days.
doneWhen: Each selected account passed a controlled drill within the last 90 days, with the result and date recorded; failed checks stay open.

steps.title: Create or Correct Emergency Access Accounts
steps.why: Emergency access accounts give your team another way into the tenant when normal administrator sign-in fails. Checking their roles, authentication and exclusions helps uncover recovery routes that exist on paper but would fail when needed.

decision.label: Emergency access accounts
decision.help: Add every account that exists only for this purpose; two are needed. IAMAI nominated these from names, roles and exclusions; a nomination is not a choice, so no account is emergency access until you choose it here and save.

whatToDo.lead: Choose the emergency access accounts below and save, then clear what Readiness lists.
create: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Users → New user. Name it so the purpose is obvious ({exampleName}).
Sign-in address on the tenant's own onmicrosoft.com domain; cloud-only; no licence; no department, title or manager.
Roles → assign Global Administrator, active and permanent.

Set a passphrase of at least 20 random characters. Store it offline in two places that different people can reach without signing in to this tenant, for example a sealed envelope in a safe and a second copy with the business owner. Never in a mailbox, a chat, or a password manager that needs this tenant to sign in.
Register a hardware security key (FIDO2) for each account and keep it with the passphrase. Not a passkey in Authenticator: that lives on a person's phone. Do not share a key between accounts.

lockedOut.label: If a change locks you out
steps: Sign in with one of the emergency accounts above, in a private browser window.
Entra admin center → Entra ID → Conditional Access → Policies → open the policy that changed today → Enable policy: Report-only (or Off) → Save. It applies within minutes.

If the portal itself is blocked: sign in from a device and network the policies trust (a managed laptop on the office network), or from any device run Connect-MgGraph -Scopes Policy.ReadWrite.ConditionalAccess and then Update-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy -ConditionalAccessPolicyId <id> -State enabledForReportingButNotEnforced.
If no route works, Microsoft support can help; they will ask for the tenant id: {tenantId}.

steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Authentication methods → Policies → Passkey (FIDO2) → Enable: On; Target: All users, keeping the existing groups and exclusions.
Allow self-service set up: Yes. Enforce attestation: Yes; it applies to new registrations only.

Save. Then Microsoft Authenticator → Enable: On, All users, for push and codes; passkeys in the app are governed by the Passkey (FIDO2) policy above.

Temporary Access Pass → Enable: On for the people who may need a pass to register their first passkey; keep the tenant's lifetime and one-time-use settings unless your security team approved different values.

steps.title: Use Separate Accounts for Admin Work
steps.why: Using a separate admin account reduces the exposure of privileged access to everyday mail, meetings and browsing. Verify the replacement account before removing access from the old one.

who.lead: {n} people hold a directory role and use that same account for mail or Teams since {from}:

whatToDo.lead: For each person:
steps: Create a second, cloud-only account for the role, named so the purpose is obvious (adm- and their name); no licence, no mailbox.
Register a passkey or security key on the admin account before its first use; the admin policies require one.

Assign the role to the admin account under the same governance model, keeping PIM eligibility where the everyday account used it: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Roles and administrators → the role → Add assignment.
Sign in with the admin account and complete the admin task it needs; only then remove the role from the everyday account.
Keep mail, Teams and files on the everyday account; open admin portals with the admin account only.

doneWhen: No account with a directory role shows mail or Teams sign-ins in the records IAMAI reads.
Verify after the change: each new admin account holds the intended role under the same governance model and has a tested sign-in path before the everyday account loses the role.
steps.ifWrong: Put the role back on the everyday account; nothing else changes.

risks.text: An admin who keeps doing admin work from the everyday account never sees the separation; moving the role is what makes it real.

helpDesk: An admin refused by a portal on the everyday account: the role moved; sign in with the admin account.
more.manager: Admin work moves to accounts that do nothing else, so a phished mailbox is not a phished tenant. Without this, every admin inbox is a way in to every setting.

steps.aiFocus: Distinguish direct roles from PIM and keep the staged handover. Historical mail or Teams events do not mean a completed migration failed.

A trusted network that lists a whole ISP range trusts every customer on it.

whatToDo.lead: Security defaults provide Microsoft's default identity protections on this licence. Check the requirements first, then turn them on if this is the chosen approach.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Overview → Properties → Manage security defaults.
Enabled → Save.
Tell people they may be asked to set up an authentication method, and give anyone who cannot a way to reach IT support.

doneWhen: Security defaults report Enabled, and everyone who holds a role has registered a method.
Verify after the change: representative administrator and user sign-ins work.
steps.aiFocus: Explain the selected protection model and observed setup gaps. Do not confuse enabling Security Defaults with customizing Conditional Access.

whatToDo.lead: Create two emergency accounts and test them before anything else on this list can lock somebody out.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Users → New user, twice: cloud-only, on the tenant's onmicrosoft.com domain, with no licence.
Give each one permanent, active Global Administrator access and an independent strong sign-in method; store the credentials where authorized staff can reach them without signing in to this tenant.
Sign in with each account, complete an administrative check, and record the date. Security defaults offer no per-user exclusions, so check how your protection model treats these accounts.

doneWhen: Two emergency accounts exist and each has signed in at least once.
Verify after the change: each account's authentication and administrative access were tested, and authorized staff can reach its credentials without a working sign-in to this tenant.
steps.aiFocus: Do not present a password and a past sign-in as complete emergency readiness. Distinguish Security Defaults from a CA design with exclusions.

whatToDo.lead: Find what still authenticates the old way, so blocking it later does not break a needed service.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Monitoring & health → Sign-in logs, and add the Client app column.
Filter the records you have (up to 30 days) to legacy clients: Exchange ActiveSync, IMAP, POP, SMTP, Other clients.
For every account that appears, find the application behind it and its owner, and ask owners about jobs that run only occasionally.
Record a supported replacement or retirement for each, and test it before blocking access.

doneWhen: The available sign-in records show no successful legacy-client sign-in, or every one left has a named owner and a recorded replacement or outstanding action.
steps.aiFocus: Report the actual evidence window and unresolved dependencies. Do not claim thirty days of coverage when the records do not contain it.

whatToDo.lead: App passwords let older applications sign in without an interactive MFA check. Replace each dependency before retiring the credential.
steps: Ask users and application owners which applications use app passwords; the Authentication methods policy is not an inventory of them.
Move each application to supported authentication and test it.
Remove the affected app passwords through Microsoft's supported user or administrative process.
Separately review the setting that allows new app passwords in the per-user MFA service settings.

doneWhen: The reviewed applications no longer depend on app passwords, and the affected app passwords are removed.
Verify after the change: creating new app passwords is disabled where that applies.
steps.aiFocus: Distinguish per-user credentials from tenant method-policy settings. Do not invent a complete app-password inventory from unavailable data.

whatToDo.lead: Keep MFA enforced while you move it from the per-user setting to the replacement you choose.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Authentication methods → Policies → Manage migration → Migration in progress.
Under Policies, enable every method people actually use, so nobody loses the one they have.
Confirm the replacement MFA protection is enabled and covers each account before changing that account's per-user MFA state.
Entra admin center → Entra ID → Users → Per-user MFA: set an account to Disabled only once its replacement protection is in place; keep the existing setting where no replacement exists.
Manage migration → Migration complete.

doneWhen: The tenant reports Migration complete, and no account is left Enabled or Enforced for per-user MFA.
Verify after the change: every account whose per-user MFA was disabled is covered by enabled replacement protection.
steps.aiFocus: Explain why a completed methods migration is not permission to disable every user's MFA state.

whatToDo.lead: Give each admin a separate account for privileged work, and test it before moving access.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Users → New user, one per person who holds a directory role, with no mailbox licence.
Register a strong method on the new account and assign the role under the same governance model, keeping eligibility where the role was eligible.
Test sign-in and the admin task with the new account; only then remove the role from the everyday account.

doneWhen: Every directory role is held by an account with no mailbox, and no everyday account holds one.
Verify after the change: each new admin account has a tested sign-in and the admin access it needs.
steps.aiFocus: Preserve eligibility versus permanent assignment. Do not treat historical productivity events as proof the migration is incomplete.

whatToDo.lead: Global Administrator has broad authority. Keep it only where the work needs it.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Roles & admins → Global Administrator: list active and eligible holders and why each needs the role.
Where a narrower role is enough, assign and test it before removing Global Administrator.
Keep the selected emergency accounts; they are counted here and they are the way back in.
Record the reason for each retained assignment.

doneWhen: Between two and four accounts hold Global Administrator, the emergency accounts among them, and everyone else holds a narrower role.
Verify after the change: each retained assignment has a current reason; a count alone does not prove least privilege.
steps.aiFocus: Treat counts as review signals, not proof. Separate emergency accounts, eligible access and day-to-day administration.

whatToDo.lead: Review guest access with the people who sponsor it, so access that is no longer needed ends through the proper process.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Users, filter User type to Guest, and add the Creation time and Last sign-in columns.
For each guest, confirm the sponsor and whether the work still needs the access.
Check pending invitations with whoever sent them; a pending invitation is not automatically obsolete.
Remove access that is no longer needed through your organization's offboarding and retention process.

doneWhen: Every reviewed guest or invitation has a confirmed purpose, or an approved removal that has been completed.
steps.aiFocus: Distinguish pending, inactive and unsupported evidence. Do not infer approval to delete from a missing sponsor field.

whatToDo.lead: Review accounts with no recent sign-in and confirm whether they are still needed.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Users, add the Last sign-in column, and sort by it.
For each account with no sign-in for 90 days or none on record, check its owner, purpose and any seasonal or service use; missing activity is a reason to check, not proof it is unused.
Block sign-in only on accounts confirmed as no longer needed; handle deletion and data retention through your separate offboarding process.

doneWhen: No enabled account has gone 90 days without a sign-in, or each one that has is recorded as deliberately kept.
Verify after the change: each blocked account was confirmed as no longer needed.
steps.aiFocus: Do not conclude missing dates mean unused accounts or invent a deletion deadline.

whatToDo.lead: Move people from text and voice codes to a stronger approved method, and test it before retiring the old one.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Authentication methods → Policies: enable the approved replacement method (Microsoft Authenticator or passkeys) for the intended users.
Help people on text message or voice call register the replacement and complete a successful sign-in with it.
Review recovery needs and application dependencies, then disable Text message and Voice call through the approved method-policy change.

doneWhen: Text message and voice call are off in the authentication methods policy, and everyone who used them has registered Authenticator or a passkey.
Verify after the change: each of them signed in with the replacement, and the agreed recovery path is preserved.
steps.aiFocus: Distinguish stronger MFA from phishing-resistant MFA. Do not claim all Authenticator modes are phishing-resistant.
